📚 Groundwater Governance: Developments and Advances

Iran's water crisis is no longer a matter of the future; we see its signs today in the drying up of wetlands, land subsidence, and the depletion of groundwater reserves. Years of unchecked extraction from aquifers have consumed resources that, for many, may take decades or even centuries to replenish.

The book "Groundwater Governance: Developments and Advances" takes an interdisciplinary look at one of the most important yet least visible aspects of the water crisis: groundwater — resources that remain unseen, yet the lives, agriculture, and food security of communities depend on them.

By examining the experiences of various countries, this book demonstrates that protecting groundwater is not achievable through isolated projects alone; it requires scientific management, sound policymaking, and cooperation among government, local communities, and consumers.

▪️Iran's water crisis, rather than being a crisis of water scarcity, may be a crisis of water management.

Are the gods dead? Has the secularization of societies in the modern era really eliminated religions? In this episode, Jabar Rahmani, a professor of the anthropology of religion, argues that contrary to popular belief, Iranians still lead religious lives; and religions, in their various manifestations, give meaning and direction to social life—even if they are not Abrahamic religions.

According to Jabar Rahmani, although surveys show that the formal forms of religiosity have weakened over recent decades, informal forms of religiosity remain prominent in society and manifest through collective rituals.

He speaks of the need for religious forms grounded in solidarity and coexistence in order to preserve the integrity and peaceful living of Iranian life.

Source: @fazelimohammadir

Gentlemen in charge! A society squeezed economically by war, sanctions, and siege becomes more sensitive, more on edge, and more vulnerable. The smallest social friction in such an environment carries a far higher cost than under normal conditions. A family grappling with inflation, job insecurity, anxiety over medicine, housing, and their children's future has far less capacity to absorb new tensions. At this point, the quality of social policy is directly linked to the country's ability to navigate the crisis. Every policy must be measured by a simple question: Does this policy, at this moment, strengthen social bonds or further inflame existing fractures? Provocative identity debates, cultural disputes such as hijab, the proposal to lash a female singer, the widespread criminalization of social behavior, measures that pit parts of society against other parts, and the reopening of cases like women's dress code are not merely cultural or legal matters. Under crisis conditions, these policies carry a secondary consequence as well: they divert part of society's political, disciplinary, and psychological energy away from the main problem and activate divisions that — you must accept — Iranian society has moved past and the people deserve respect for, yet under economic pressure these divisions have the potential to turn into social fractures. In this sense, a country in crisis needs something akin to a "social ceasefire" — meaning preventing the creation of conflicts that are not urgent and that can drain the country's limited social capital.

Security from Beyond Borders: The Necessity of the Axis of Resistance for Iran

Hadi Masoumi-Zare, a researcher of Middle Eastern studies, is a guest on IranTalk in this episode to discuss Iran's regional presence and the Axis of Resistance. Masoumi-Zare traces the genealogy of Iran's regional presence back to the Median period and shows that regional ties were one of the main factors that historically preserved the security of the Iranian homeland. Watch the conversation: https://youtu.be/1Bk_7Tcq0rY

He also believes that in recent centuries, due to Iran's cultural, religious, and linguistic distinctiveness compared to neighboring countries, Iran has suffered from a kind of strategic loneliness that doubles the necessity of regional ties.

Therefore, in Masoumi-Zare's view, any form of government established in the Iranian homeland must pursue security before all else from beyond the borders.
